Kibble, Cooked or Raw: Which Diet Gives the Best Dog Poop?

Poop amount, smell and firmness can change from one diet to another, but no single diet gives every dog the "best" poop. The right diet for your dog is the one they eat well, that keeps their poop consistently healthy, and that keeps their weight and energy steady.

How poop can differ by diet (general tendencies)

DietAmountSmellFirmness
Dry kibbleVaries a lot with ingredients and fiber. High-fiber food tends to mean more poop.Varies by food.Usually fairly consistent. Can get hard if your dog doesn't drink enough water.
Cooked (home-cooked or fresh-cooked)Easily digested ingredients can mean less poop; lots of vegetables can mean more.Depends on the ingredients.More moisture, so it can be a little softer.
RawOften said to be smaller.Often said to smell less.Tends to be firm. With a lot of bone, it can turn white and crumbly.

These are only commonly reported tendencies. Even on the same diet, poop can vary widely with the ingredients, the ratios and your dog's own body. Less poop isn't automatically better, either.

Pros and cons of each diet

DietProsWatch out for
Dry kibbleEasy to find a complete, nutritionally balanced food, and easy to store and serve.Low in moisture, so make sure your dog drinks plenty of water.
CookedHigh in moisture, and many dogs love it.Home-cooked meals are hard to balance nutritionally. It's best to go over recipes with your vet.
RawMany dogs love it.Bacterial hygiene risks, nutritional balance, and constipation or foreign-body risks from bones.

Raw feeding: don't skip the hygiene

Uncooked meat can carry bacteria such as Salmonella. Dogs can shed bacteria in their poop even without symptoms, so homes with babies, older adults or anyone with a weakened immune system need to be extra careful.

  • Wash your hands, cutting boards and bowls right after preparing it.
  • Don't leave uneaten raw food sitting out.
  • Pick up poop right away and wash your hands afterward.
  • If you feed bones, check the size and amount with your vet.

What to watch when switching diets

  • Whatever the diet, don't switch overnight. Mix the new food into the old one a little at a time over 7 to 10 days. The mixing chart is in how to help your dog have healthy poop.
  • Log your dog's poop every day during the switch. You can check firmness and color with the dog poop color and firmness chart.
  • If soft poop keeps coming, go back one step. If diarrhea lasts more than a day, read causes of diarrhea in dogs and see your vet.
  • If white, hard poop keeps showing up, suspect the bone ratio. Also see why dog poop turns yellow or gray.

Bottom line: the right answer is different for every dog

When choosing a diet, look beyond poop to weight, coat, energy, age and any health conditions. Puppies, seniors and dogs with health conditions in particular should see a vet before changing diets.

This article is general reference information, not a diagnosis. If your dog seems low on energy or has symptoms that worry you, talk to your vet.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which gives the best poop: kibble, cooked or raw?

There's no answer that fits every dog. The right diet is the one your dog eats well, that keeps their poop consistently healthy, and that keeps their weight and energy steady.

My dog's poop comes out white on a raw diet.

A high bone or calcium ratio can make poop white and crumbly. It can easily lead to constipation, so talk to your vet about the bone ratio.

My dog's poop got soft after starting cooked food.

The switch may have been too fast, or the food may be high in moisture or fat. Switch more slowly, and if it stays soft for more than a day, talk to your vet.

Is raw feeding dangerous?

Uncooked meat can carry bacteria, so careful hygiene is a must. There are also nutritional-balance and bone-related risks, so it's best to talk to your vet before starting.
